title: Texaco, Inc. v. Pennzoil Co.
lead: A proposed Getty Oil transaction reaches board approval and a public announcement, then Texaco’s competing deal produces a jury finding that it knowingly induced breach of an existing Pennzoil agreement.

actors.name: Pennzoil and chief executive Hugh Liedtke
actors.role: Prospective acquirer claiming an agreement reached at the January 3 board meeting.

actors.name: Getty Oil and its board
actors.role: Company whose approval and later withdrawal were central to formation and breach.

actors.name: Gordon Getty and the Sarah C. Getty Trust
actors.role: Trustee and holder of about 40.2 percent of Getty Oil shares.

actors.name: J. Paul Getty Museum
actors.role: Holder of about 11.8 percent of shares and participant in the competing transactions.

actors.name: Texaco
actors.role: Competing acquirer and defendant in the intentional-interference action.

proceedings: A Texas jury awarded Pennzoil $7.53 billion compensatory and $3 billion punitive damages.
The Texas appellate court rejected the principal liability, trial-error, and compensation challenges.
It conditionally required a $2 billion punitive remittitur within thirty days: reformed affirmance if filed, otherwise reversal and remand.
limits: The court applied agreed New York substantive and Texas procedural law. Its disposition was conditional, and several defenses failed procedurally rather than on their merits. Later bankruptcy and a $3 billion settlement belong to the assigned editorial subsequent history, not this appellate judgment.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Getty’s ownership dispute opens a negotiating opportunity
paragraphs: Gordon Getty, as trustee of the Sarah C. Getty Trust, controlled approximately 40.2 percent of Getty Oil’s shares, and the J. Paul Getty Museum held about 11.8 percent. Disagreement between Gordon and company management created an opportunity for a transaction giving Gordon and Pennzoil control and potentially dividing assets.

Pennzoil began with a late-December 1983 public tender offer of $100 per share. A memorandum negotiated around January 1–2 proposed acquiring the Museum’s shares, giving Pennzoil three-sevenths and leaving the Trust four-sevenths. If restructuring was not agreed by December 31, 1984, assets would be divided by those interests. Gordon, the Museum, and Pennzoil signed; Getty Oil did not, and its board initially rejected the price.

sources.pinpoint: Facts and bargaining chronology; 729 S.W.2d at 784–786

sections.title: Price negotiations lead to a board vote and asserted acceptance
sections.cue: Why did the parties later dispute the significance of formal papers?
paragraphs: On January 3 Pennzoil offered $110 per share plus a contingent payment related to Getty Oil’s ERC interest. The Museum’s lawyer indicated acceptance of $110 and a deferred $5 if the deal was firm. The board voted fifteen to one for a proposal involving that $5 payment. During a recess, Pennzoil chief executive Hugh Liedtke accepted the counterproposal, and that acceptance reached the board before adjournment.

Participants also discussed management protections. Pennzoil relied on congratulations and public announcements as manifestations of a completed agreement. Getty’s January 4 release called it an agreement in principle, subject to a definitive merger agreement, shareholder approval, and regulatory requirements. Lawyers continued drafting implementation documents. Pennzoil regarded those papers as implementing a present obligation; Texaco later argued that execution and unresolved details prevented any obligation.

sections.title: Texaco obtains the Getty participants’ commitments
sections.cue: What evidence supported active interference rather than merely a competing offer?
paragraphs: Getty’s investment banker meanwhile solicited bidders. Texaco advisers assessed how to stop Pennzoil’s transaction, identifying the Museum as a key first target and Gordon’s concern about retaining control as another source of leverage. Texaco offered more, obtained Museum and Trust agreements, and arranged a Getty merger.

The Museum demanded protection from Pennzoil-related claims and would not assure Texaco that its agreement breached no prior contract. Getty withdrew from the Pennzoil arrangement and proceeded with Texaco. These events were disputed at trial; the appellate court later examined evidentiary support for the jury, not every conflict as an original factfinder.

Pennzoil sued for knowing interference. Texaco denied a contract or knowledge of one, citing the missing Getty signature, formal-execution language, complexity, unsettled terms, and assurances from lawyers and participants. A Texas jury found for Pennzoil and awarded $7.53 billion compensation and $3 billion punitive damages. The parties agreed to New York substantive and Texas procedural law.

sources.pinpoint: Facts; Positions; Court and stage; 729 S.W.2d at 784–787,796–805

sections.title: The appellate court sustains the finding of present agreement
sections.cue: How did each formation consideration bear on the record?
paragraphs: Justice Warren wrote for Warren, Jack Smith, and Sam Bass. Under New York law, objective intent controlled. An express reservation against obligation before signature could be decisive, but merely anticipating a later writing did not preclude present assent. The court considered reservation, partial performance, essential terms, and customary formality together.

The memorandum’s board-approval condition could be satisfied by January 3. The press release’s conditions could concern consummation rather than formation, and “agreement in principle” had a disputed business meaning. Draft execution clauses had to be read with present-commitment language. Those materials did not conclusively foreclose the jury’s reading.

There was little partial performance beyond preliminary Pennzoil financing. The court did not invent completed joint performance, but the short interval before withdrawal reduced the force of inactivity. Evidence supported agreement on price, ownership shares, the Museum sale, and restructuring or division. Changing the purchaser of Museum shares for tax reasons could be implementation. ERC payment, dividends, a restored price-protection clause, and employee provisions likewise had to be assessed against contemporaneous assent; later draft changes did not alone disprove an earlier bargain.

Magnitude and complexity strongly favored formal documentation but were not conclusive alongside signatures, board action, and conduct. The court also rejected indefiniteness: reasonable certainty had to permit identification of breach and remedy, not specify every implementing detail.

sections.title: Knowledge of operative facts supports interference despite contrary legal advice
sections.cue: Which defenses were actually resolved on the merits?
paragraphs: Knowledge required awareness of facts producing the contractual duty, not accurate legal classification or every detail. Lawyer assurances could be weighed against documents, announcements, transaction planning, communications, and indemnity demands; they did not automatically defeat liability. The court found sufficient circumstantial support.

Inducement required more than contracting with someone already bound. The planned Museum-and-Trust sequence, favorable terms, and protections supported active persuasion. Getty’s prior dissatisfaction and pursuit of bids did not necessarily eliminate causation. Competition did not privilege interference with the existing, nonterminable contract found by the jury.

Mutual mistake and statute-of-frauds defenses failed for pleading and submission defects; the court did not decide that the unsigned memorandum satisfied every statutory writing requirement. The Securities and Exchange Commission restriction on outside purchases during a tender offer protected tendering shareholders and allowed exemptions. Texaco had not shown an automatically void contract it could invoke. The fiduciary-duty challenge also failed: Gordon’s ownership did not conclusively establish legal control, valuation evidence existed, and a later higher offer did not itself prove the earlier bargain unlawful. The court distinguished Revlon’s sequence and circumstances.

sources.pinpoint: Knowing interference and validity defenses; 729 S.W.2d at 796–809,829–831

sections.title: The court reviews the jury charge and trial objections separately
sections.cue: Why did rejection of appellate arguments not validate every challenged event?
paragraphs: Broad-form submission did not assume a contract or omit knowing interference. Intentional refusal to ascertain facts or bad faith differed from negligent failure to investigate. Good-faith language concerned performance after agreement, not mere prospective relations. Some objections to wording, emphasis, or balance were unpreserved or inadequately briefed.

Evidence rulings were tested for harmful error. Some business-experience and perception testimony was admissible; several documents or statements were improperly admitted but harmless because cumulative, repeated in proper testimony, or introduced or used by Texaco itself. Other exclusion claims involving later SEC discussion, a Delaware pleading, and legal advice failed under relevance and cumulative-evidence reasoning.

The court rejected challenges concerning counsel’s contribution to Judge Farris, replacement by Judge Casseb when Farris became ill, denial of a new-trial hearing, alleged juror misconduct, and retirement qualifications. It found no demonstrated bias or pecuniary interest, prejudicial substitution, or sufficiently supported outside influence or concealment. Quo warranto, not collateral recusal, was required to attack the certified retired judge’s authority. Supremacy, commerce, and due-process objections were untimely; full faith and credit failed because New York law had been applied. These were historical procedural rulings, not findings that every suggested defense lost on its substance.

sources.pinpoint: Instructions, evidence, trial objections; 729 S.W.2d at 809–859 & nn.1–2

sections.title: Compensation follows the lost access to oil reserves
sections.cue: What evidence supported the multibillion-dollar figure?
paragraphs: The court permitted pecuniary loss of contractual benefits and appropriate consequential loss for intentional interference. Pennzoil sought access to reserves, not simply a minority stock trade. Experts estimated 1.008 billion barrels of oil equivalent and a $7.47 gap between $10.87 replacement cost and $3.40 acquisition cost, producing about $7.53 billion. Texaco cross-examined but offered no competing expert.

The court sustained reliance on that evidence despite disputes over crude quality, the five-year cost period, development costs, taxes, and ultimate division. It treated the lost interest as present loss and independently found the requested present-value instruction unpreserved. It upheld prejudgment interest under New York’s rule for inducing breach.

sections.title: The punitive reduction produces a conditional result
sections.cue: Give both branches of the appellate disposition.
paragraphs: Intentional, willful, wanton disregard permitted punitive damages. Economic self-interest, absence of personal hatred, and legal advice were not categorical defenses; advice remained a factor, not an automatic bar. The $3 billion figure was not excessive merely because it was about forty percent of compensation. Still, considering conduct, deterrence, and New York’s more conservative approach, the court found $1 billion sufficient and $2 billion excessive.

If Pennzoil filed a $2 billion remittitur within thirty days, the court would reform and affirm for $7.53 billion compensation and $1 billion exemplary damages. Otherwise it would reverse and remand. It refused the requested certification to the Texas Supreme Court. The preserved report records later rehearing denials without another opinion.

The assigned “Of Oil and Honor” note describes later bankruptcy and a $3 billion settlement. Those are editorial subsequent history, not the conditional disposition of this February 1987 opinion or an independently reviewed additional case.

sources.pinpoint: Conditional disposition; Assigned account; 729 S.W.2d at 768,836–837,863–866; casebook 190–191
